items.title: AWS CodeDeploy Can Now Restart Your EC2 Fleet — Here’s Why It Matters
items.author: Frank Mbelu
items.content:
A practical look at AWS’s new RESTART deployment mode and where I think it makes sense.

I’ve worked around EC2-based infrastructure enough to know that restarting a fleet sounds easier than it actually is.

Restarting an instance can be trivial. Restarting a production fleet without creating an availability problem is a whole different conversation.

AWS just introduced a new RESTART deployment mode for CodeDeploy.

At first glance, it sounds like a small feature.

It is.

But if you’re managing EC2 fleets with CodeDeploy, this solves a fairly common operational problem: restarting instances without having to build another script around the process.

Before this, teams could redeploy the current application revision or create their own scripts to restart instances.

Now CodeDeploy has a dedicated option for it.

Why does restarting a fleet need its own deployment mode?

Restarting one EC2 instance is easy.

aws ec2 reboot-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxx

The problem starts when you have 50 or 100 instances serving production traffic.

You don’t want to restart everything at once.

You need to think about:

  • How many instances should restart at the same time?
  • Is enough capacity available while the restart happens?
  • Is the application healthy after the restart?
  • What happens if one batch fails?
  • Should the operation stop if a CloudWatch alarm fires?
  • How do you know exactly what happened?

You can write a script to handle all of this.

But now you have another piece of operational automation to maintain.

That’s where the new RESTART deployment mode becomes useful.

AWS introduced the feature on October 5, 2026, specifically for EC2 and on-premises in-place deployments.

What does RESTART actually do?

The important detail is that CodeDeploy doesn’t deploy a new application version.

Instead, it uses the last successful revision associated with the deployment group.

You don’t provide a new revision when creating the deployment.

For example:

aws deploy create-deployment \
    --application-name MyApp \
    --deployment-group-name MyDeploymentGroup \
    --deployment-mode RESTART \
    --description "Restart application instances"

The RESTART mode tells CodeDeploy to restart the application on the target instances using that deployment group's last successful revision. You don't specify --revision for this type of deployment.

That’s a useful distinction.

You’re not saying:

Deploy version 27 again.

You’re saying:

Restart these instances using the revision they’re already supposed to be running.

The part I find most useful

The biggest benefit isn’t the restart itself.

It’s that the restart stays inside CodeDeploy.

That means you can continue using the deployment controls you already have configured.

For example:

  • Deployment configuration
  • Lifecycle hooks
  • Health validation
  • CloudWatch alarms
  • Rollback configuration
  • Deployment history

So instead of having:

Production deployment
        |
   CodeDeploy
Production restart
        |
Random automation script

you can have:

Production deployment
        |
     CodeDeploy
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
Deploy     Restart

That’s a much cleaner operational model.

Where I would use it

Imagine an application running across three EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.

              Application Load Balancer
                           |
              +------------+------------+
              |            |            |
            EC2-1        EC2-2        EC2-3
              |
              v
        AWS CodeDeploy
              |
              v
       Restart in batches
              |
              v
        Health validation
              |
        +-----+------+
        |            |
     Healthy       Failed
        |            |
        v            v
   Next batch    Stop/rollback

Rather than restarting the entire fleet simultaneously, CodeDeploy can process the instances according to the deployment configuration.

For example:

Batch 1
EC2-1 → restart → validate

Batch 2
EC2-2 → restart → validate

Batch 3
EC2-3 → restart → validate

This is the important difference between:

“reboot these machines”

and

“perform a controlled operational change to this production fleet.”

There’s also a performance benefit

AWS reported some interesting results from its testing.

In one test involving 50 EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, the restart deployment completed in 82.6 seconds, compared with 507.4 seconds for a standard deployment.

That’s about a 6.1× speed improvement in that particular test.

Obviously, I wouldn’t take that number and assume every environment will see the same result.

The actual improvement depends on things like fleet size, revision size, deployment configuration, lifecycle hooks and the CodeDeploy agent version.

The reason for the improvement is more interesting.

With CodeDeploy agent 2.1.0 or newer, the agent can reuse the existing copy of the revision already present on the instance instead of downloading it again. If the local copy is missing or incomplete, the agent can fall back to downloading the revision.

That’s a sensible optimisation for a restart operation.

The lifecycle still matters

A restart isn’t simply:

Stop process
    ↓
Start process

CodeDeploy still runs the application lifecycle around the operation.

The AWS documentation shows the workflow as:

ApplicationStop
      ↓
DownloadBundle
      ↓
BeforeInstall
      ↓
Install
      ↓
AfterInstall
      ↓
ApplicationStart
      ↓
ValidateService

The Install phase can reapply the revision and correct drift in managed files.

That gives you another useful property: a restart can also bring managed application files back into the expected state.

One important limitation

There’s a detail here that I would pay close attention to in production.

RESTART does not run CodeDeploy’s load balancer BlockTraffic and AllowTraffic steps.

The instance remains registered with the load balancer while the application stops and starts.

That means you shouldn’t assume CodeDeploy will automatically drain traffic for you during the restart.

For a request-serving application, your application and lifecycle hooks need to handle this properly.

For example, ApplicationStop should stop accepting new work and give in-flight requests an opportunity to complete before the process exits.

This is one of those details that could easily get missed if you only read the announcement headline.

CloudWatch alarms are still useful

Another reason I like this approach is that you don’t lose the operational controls already available in CodeDeploy.

CodeDeploy can monitor the CloudWatch alarms configured for the deployment group.

If an alarm enters the ALARM state during the deployment, CodeDeploy can stop the restart according to the configured deployment behaviour.

That gives you something a basic restart script usually doesn’t have.

A script might do this:

Restart instance
       ↓
Wait 60 seconds
       ↓
Restart next instance

CodeDeploy gives you the opportunity to make the decision based on actual deployment health.

That’s a much better model.

This could also be useful for automated remediation

This is where I think the feature gets more interesting.

Imagine you have a JVM service where memory usage gradually increases over time.

You could build something like:

CloudWatch Alarm
       |
       v
   EventBridge
       |
       v
     Lambda
       |
       v
CodeDeploy RESTART
       |
       v
   EC2 fleet

For example, a CloudWatch alarm could detect a condition that your operational runbook already considers safe to remediate through a controlled restart.

EventBridge could trigger Lambda, and Lambda could call CreateDeployment with:

deploymentMode = RESTART

AWS specifically highlights this type of automated remediation as a potential use case.

I would still put guardrails around it.

Automation without guardrails is just a faster way to create an outage.

What I would check before using it

I wouldn’t immediately replace every restart script in production.

I’d start with a staging deployment group.

I’d verify:

  1. The CodeDeploy agent version.
  2. The last successful deployment revision.
  3. The deployment configuration.
  4. ApplicationStop and ApplicationStart behaviour.
  5. Application health checks.
  6. CloudWatch alarms.
  7. Minimum healthy capacity.
  8. How long the application takes to become healthy after a restart
  9. What happens if the restart fails halfway through.

Then I’d run a controlled restart and inspect the CodeDeploy deployment history.

The current AWS documentation requires the deployment group to have a successful deployment because RESTART needs a previous successful revision to reapply.

There are a few constraints

RESTART is currently limited to EC2 and on-premises in-place deployments.

It does not support:

  • Amazon ECS deployment groups
  • AWS Lambda deployment groups

You also cannot provide a new revision with a RESTART deployment, and you cannot combine it with updateOutdatedInstancesOnly=true.

So this isn’t a replacement for normal deployments.

It’s a separate operational capability for restarting an existing fleet.

A small AWS feature, but a useful one

Not every AWS announcement needs to change the way you architect your infrastructure.

Sometimes the useful features are much smaller.

For teams still running EC2 workloads with CodeDeploy, I think this is one of those features worth testing.

The value isn’t that AWS can restart an EC2 instance.

We’ve been able to do that for years.

The value is being able to treat restarting a production fleet as a controlled CodeDeploy operation rather than maintaining another custom script around the side.

You get the deployment configuration, lifecycle hooks, health validation, alarm monitoring and deployment history that are already part of CodeDeploy.

And if you’re running CodeDeploy agent 2.1.0 or newer, you can also benefit from local revision reuse during the restart.

It’s a relatively small feature.

But it’s the kind of small feature that can make day-to-day infrastructure operations cleaner.

My take: this isn’t a revolutionary CodeDeploy feature, and I don’t think it needs to be. It’s a practical improvement that removes one more reason to maintain custom operational scripts around EC2 fleets. If I were already using CodeDeploy for an EC2 workload, I’d definitely test RESTART before building another restart workflow myself.

items.title: The Night I Stopped Trusting “It Works on My Machine”
items.author: Frank Mbelu
items.content:
A Django app running locally can fool you.

Pages load. Logs look clean. You feel done.

Then production reality arrives: one instance gets noisy, traffic shifts unexpectedly, health checks fail, and suddenly your “working app” is just a fragile script with good branding.

This project started when I realised I didn’t want to ship demos anymore.
I wanted to build a Django platform that behaves like a real system under stress.

The Build

I designed a highly available AWS platform around one principle: assume failure, then design anyway.

So I built:

  • A 3-tier VPC (public, private, database subnets)
  • Multi-AZ deployment for compute and database
  • ALB with health checks in front of Django (Gunicorn + Nginx)
  • Auto Scaling based on CPU thresholds
  • RDS PostgreSQL with failover
  • CloudWatch alarms + SNS notifications
  • Secure instance access through Session Manager
  • A Kubernetes path on EKS (Helm + HPA)
  • Prometheus and Grafana for visibility
  • GitHub Actions for Docker build automation

Not flashy. Just be deliberate.

What Changed for Me

Before this, I thought DevOps was mostly about tooling.

After this, I see it as operational empathy.

You’re building for:

  • the engineer who gets paged at 2am,
  • the user who doesn’t care why your app is down,
  • and your future self, who will forget today’s assumptions.

Infrastructure as Code (Terraform and CloudFormation) gave me more than automation.
It gave me honesty. Every design decision had to be explicit, reviewable, and repeatable.

The Hard Truths

  1. High availability is expensive by default.
    Redundancy, NAT gateways, managed databases, monitoring: resilience has a bill.
  2. Security posture is never "finished".
    Least privilege, subnet isolation, and private access patterns are a baseline, not a badge.
  3. Observability is part of the product.
    If you can’t see failure clearly, you don’t actually have reliability.

What’s Next

If I push this further, I’d prioritise:

  • stronger secrets handling everywhere,
  • deeper defense layers (WAF, tighter IAM boundaries),
  • and a full CI/CD path from build to deployment, not just image publishing.

This project opened my eyes to a simple rule I now trust:

Don’t build for the best-case path. Build for the day things break.

Because they will.

Repo: https://github.com/franklynux/aws-django-ha-platform

The Night I Stopped Trusting “It Works on My Machine” was originally published in AWS in Plain English on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Kubernetes Is Moving On: Understanding the Shift From Ingress to Gateway API
items.author: Frank Mbelu
items.content:
Over the years, Kubernetes has grown from a container orchestrator into the backbone of modern cloud platforms. With that growth, some parts of the ecosystem have struggled to keep up. One of those is the traditional Ingress model. It has served the community well, but it is now reaching the end of its lifecycle. The Kubernetes community is guiding everyone toward the Gateway API, a more flexible and modern approach to managing traffic.

This post breaks down what is changing, why it matters, and how teams can prepare.

Why Ingress Is Being Phased Out

Ingress has been the entry point for external traffic into Kubernetes clusters for a long time. It handled basic routing well, and most teams relied on it during their early Kubernetes journey.

But as workloads and architectures evolved, several limitations became impossible to ignore:

  • Ingress was too limited for complex routing and advanced traffic control.
  • Different vendors implemented Ingress differently, which created confusion.
  • Achieving advanced behavior required workarounds instead of clean solutions.
  • A single Ingress resource created bottlenecks in large or multi-team environments.

Ingress did its job, but it was not built for the scale and complexity we deal with today.

Why Gateway API Is the Better Approach

Gateway API is the result of learning from the pain points of Ingress. It is more expressive, more modular and more aligned with real organizational structures.

Some of the benefits include:

1. Clear separation of responsibilities

Platform teams can manage Gateways, while app teams manage Routes. This reduces conflict and makes governance easier.

2. True multi-tenancy

Teams can share infrastructure without interfering with each other’s configs.

3. Consistent behavior across vendors

Since the spec is more detailed, you no longer have to guess how your controller behaves.

4. Built-in support for advanced traffic patterns

Things like mTLS, header-based routing, traffic splitting, and canary strategies are first-class features.

5. Better long-term maintainability

Gateway API is actively evolving, while Ingress is no longer where new ideas are being developed.

Gateway API is simply better aligned with how modern infrastructure works.

What This Means for Teams

Ingress will not disappear immediately. There is no need for a rushed migration. However, organizations that want to stay ahead should start working Gateway API into their platform strategy.

A few practical steps to begin:

  • Start with non-critical services to get familiar with the workflow.
  • Run both Ingress and Gateway API side by side during the transition.
  • Review your routing patterns and identify where Gateway API simplifies things.
  • Keep an eye on updates from your ingress controller provider.

The earlier you embrace it, the smoother your long-term operations will be.

Final Thoughts

The shift from Ingress to Gateway API represents a natural evolution of the Kubernetes networking model. It reflects the lessons learned from real production environments and the need for more flexible, reliable, and scalable traffic management.

If this is your first time exploring Gateway API, now is a good time to start. It is already production-ready, fully supported by major vendors, and shaping the future of Kubernetes networking.

This transition is not simply a technical change. It is a chance to modernize your platform, reduce friction between teams, and take full advantage of the direction Kubernetes is heading.

About the Author

Franklyn Mbelu is a cloud and DevOps engineer who builds and supports scalable platforms on AWS. He focuses on automation, CI/CD, and cloud-native tooling and enjoys sharing practical insights to help engineers grow in their cloud journey.
